processing: Fresh leaf is graded and spread, fixed, rolled, given a first bake, shaped, worked to bring out the down, then dried. This is the sequence set for the county's protected Xiushan tea.
harvest_season: Spring. The standard calls for mostly one bud with two leaves (over 70%), picked on clear mornings, with one-bud-one-leaf and one-bud-three-leaf making up the rest.
appearance_dry: Tight, fine strips with visible tips, a moist yellow-green colour.
taste_profile: Fresh and brisk with a lasting clean aroma and a mellow finish.

brewing.notes: General guidance for a maojian-style green rather than a local rule: pour on water just below boiling and keep the first steep short, since the down and fine tips release quickly.

vintage_note: As with other Chinese greens, it is sold by the current spring harvest and is best within about a year. Expect to see it labelled as Xiushan tea (秀山茶叶), the protected county name, with maojian as the style.
description:
Xiushan Maojian is a fine, downy green tea from Xiushan, the Tujia and Miao autonomous county in the Wuling Mountains at Chongqing's southeastern edge, close to Hunan and Guizhou. It counts among the commonly named famous teas of Chongqing.

The name that carries legal protection is the broader Xiushan tea, which covers 11 townships and 109 villages, with gardens above 700 metres mixed in among forest. Maojian is best understood as the premium style of that county tea.

The making has a step many greens skip: after shaping, the leaf is worked to raise its down, which gives the strips their fine, tippy look. The cup is yellow-green, fresh and brisk, and the aroma holds up over several steeps.

The spring standard is mostly one bud with two leaves, so this is not a bud-only tea and should not be priced like one. Look for the harvest year and the geographical indication mark, and bear in mind that county tea and premium maojian can share a label.
history:
A county gazetteer from the Guangxu reign of the Qing dynasty is cited as listing Xiushan tea as tribute. Older farmers also recall teas from particular villages, Mengdong, Pingyi and Jianshan, as famous in neighbouring counties in the late Qing and early Republican years, though that rests on memory.

Xiushan tea was registered as a protected agricultural geographical indication on 16 August 2016, and in December 2020 it joined a national list of distinctive quality farm products. When the name Xiushan Maojian itself came into use is little documented.
